summary: Shenzhen shows off robots and robotaxis to APEC visitors and China pushes AI safety talks, while weak spending and falling gig wages shape life outside the showrooms.
body: With world leaders in Shenzhen for APEC, the city is showing off its robots. In what locals call "Robotics Valley", more than 200 robot companies sit within a 30-minute drive, and showrooms display over 200 machines; one store manager says about 70% of visitors now come from abroad.[^1] At the APEC CEO Summit, which drew more than 2,000 delegates, Baidu's Robin Li said its Apollo Go robotaxis run or are being tested in Dubai, London and Hong Kong, and Xiaomi's Lei Jun said humanoid robots can now work an eight-hour factory shift.[^2] These claims come from company leaders and have not been independently tested.

Officials want to shape the rules too. The chair of this year's APEC senior officials, Chen Xu, said members reached "an important consensus" on the safe use of AI and discussed the role of data for the first time.[^3] This comes as the US tightens limits on Chinese access to advanced chips, and as Chinese AI shares fell after Nvidia's leadership crisis.[^3][^5]

Away from the showrooms, daily life is harder. October data showed retail sales up just 0.4% and urban unemployment at 5.1%, and the statistics bureau said "domestic demand is still insufficient".[^4] A Shenzhen delivery driver told the BBC, as cited by Streamline, that the city is "not a magic place" anymore, and a Reuters analysis cited there found ride-hailing drivers' wages fell 1.8% in 2025.[^4]
differences: Company leaders and summit organisers present Shenzhen as a model of fast-moving technology; official data and workers quoted in foreign reports point to weak demand and squeezed incomes.[^1][^2][^4]

reads.summary: A quick tour of Shenzhen's "Robotics Valley" during APEC week: underwater arms, humanoid robots and who is coming to look.
